events.title: Howell v. Circuit Court of Indiana: In Forma Pauperis Motion Denied, Prospective Filing Bar Imposed
events.summary: The Supreme Court denied Danny Howell's motion for leave to proceed in forma pauperis and dismissed his certiorari petition. The Court imposed a prospective filing bar preventing Howell, an incarcerated petitioner serving a 70-year sentence, from filing any future in forma pauperis petitions in noncriminal matters unless he pays the full docketing fee and complies with all filing rules. Justice Jackson dissented, arguing that the routine application of such bars to indigent prisoners—who have filed only a handful of petitions over many years—impermissibly restricts access to the Court and abandons the Court's tradition of keeping its doors open to all classes of litigants.
events.why_relevant: Reflects the Court's expansion of prospective filing bars against indigent incarcerated litigants, raising constitutional concerns about equal access to judicial review and the right to petition for habeas relief.
events.basis: As the petitioner has repeatedly abused this Court's process, the Clerk is directed not to accept any further petitions in noncriminal matters from petitioner unless the docketing fee required by Rule 38(a) is paid and the petition is submitted in compliance with Rule 33.1.

This rapid expansion of the detained population has occurred concurrent with ICE's cessation of third-party medical funding and has strained facility resources, medical capacity, and mental health services. The surge in detention correlates with the sharp increase in in-custody deaths and allegations of inadequate care and inhumane conditions.
events.why_relevant: A near-doubling of the detained population without corresponding increases in medical, mental health, and safety resources creates systemic conditions that directly contribute to preventable deaths and constitutional violations.
events.basis: The detained population in ICE facilities has exploded from less than 40,000 in January 2025 to over 73,000 today.

events.title: ICE detainees dying at elevated rate in early 2026
events.summary: In the first 21 days of 2026, at least six people died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody—a pace that would yield approximately 120 deaths annually, compared to 32 deaths in all of 2025. Deaths are attributed to substandard medical care, inadequate mental health supervision, and insufficient treatment for withdrawal and chronic conditions. ICE ceased paying for third-party medical treatment on October 3, 2025, and the detained population has nearly doubled from 40,000 to over 73,000 since January 2025, straining facility resources and oversight.
events.why_relevant: Systemic failure in detention oversight and medical care represents a breakdown in government duty to protect persons in state custody and raises constitutional concerns about cruel and unusual punishment.
events.basis: In just 21 days, at least six people have died in ICE custody. Last year, ICE did not have six in-custody deaths until April 25.

events.title: Trump issues Executive Order 14377 preempting state and local permitting for Los Angeles wildfire reconstruction, directing federal agencies to replace local approval processes with self-certification requirements.
